title: Artery of Percheron infarction a rare anatomical variant and a diagnostic challenge: Case report
case_prompt: A 55-year-old man was found unconscious in front of his home and brought to the emergency department. He had no significant medical history and took no long-term medications. On arrival, his Glasgow Coma Scale score was 4. He was afebrile, blood pressure was 100/55 mm Hg, pulse 45–55 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and temperature 32.5 °C. Pupils were poorly reactive bilaterally, with a dilated right pupil. He flexed his arm and extended his leg to pain. Routine laboratory tests, including complete blood count, electrolytes, renal and liver function, and arterial blood gases, were all within normal limits. Cardiovascular exam and ECG were unremarkable. A noncontrast head CT showed no hemorrhage or ischemia. Transcranial Doppler demonstrated patency of the carotid, basilar, and vertebral arteries. He was admitted to the ICU for respiratory support. Four hours later, he regained consciousness but remained somnolent. He had bilateral ptosis, and examination revealed vertical gaze palsy. On hospital day 2, repeat CT showed bilateral paramedian thalamic hypodensities (~15 × 11 mm). CT angiography was unremarkable. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral hyperintense T2 and FLAIR signals in the paramedian thalami and rostral midbrain, with corresponding restricted diffusion on DWI and low ADC values.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Top-of-the-basilar syndrome was considered because it can cause bilateral thalamic infarcts; it was excluded since “a transcranial Doppler was performed and showed complete patency of the carotid, basilar, and vertebral arteries.”  
2. Cerebral venous thrombosis was considered because occlusion of internal cerebral veins can cause bilateral thalamic infarcts; it was excluded as “patients with cerebral venous thrombosis may present with symptoms of increased intracranial pressure such as headache, papilledema, vomiting, convulsions, aphasia, and focal neurologic deficits,” none of which were present.  
3. Chronic hypertensive encephalopathy was considered as a cause of bilateral lacunar infarcts; it was excluded because he “had no significant past medical history” of hypertension.  
4. Bilateral thalamic glioma was considered because neoplastic lesions appear hyperintense on T2/FLAIR; it was excluded since “absence of restricted diffusion” distinguishes neoplasm, whereas this patient had “bilateral paramedian thalamic hyperintense signal due to restricted diffusion.”  
5. Acute demyelinating encephalomyelitis and multiple sclerosis were considered due to T2 hyperintense thalamic lesions; they were excluded because demyelinating lesions “enhance after administration of gadolinium,” which was not observed.  
6. Extrapontine myelinolysis was considered because it can cause bilateral thalamic lesions; it was excluded as typical lesions involve the “internal and external capsules, basal ganglia such as the putamen, caudate nucleus and lateral geniculate bodies,” which were not seen here.  
7. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease was considered since it can produce bilateral thalamic hyperintensity; it was excluded because CJD lesions also involve the “putamen, caudate nuclei, periaqueductal region, occipital cortex, and white matter,” which were absent.  
8. Wernicke’s encephalopathy was considered for anoxic injury of thalami; it was excluded because Wernicke’s lesions appear around the “third ventricle, periaqueductal region, mamillary bodies and tectal plate,” none of which were present.  
9. Wilson’s disease was considered because it causes bilateral thalamic lesions; it was excluded as Wilson’s disease typically affects young adults and shows lesions in the “lentiform nucleus, thalami, globus pallidus, caudate nuclei, putamen,” plus extrapyramidal signs, which were not seen.  
10. Fahr’s disease was considered due to basal ganglia and thalamic calcifications; it was excluded because CT did not demonstrate calcifications in the “caudate and dentate nuclei, putamen, globus pallidus, and thalami.”  
11. Inflammatory and infectious etiologies (tuberculosis, malaria, meningioencephalitis, Flavi and West Nile virus) were considered for bilateral thalamic involvement; they were excluded since “patient history, specific imaging characteristics and the presence or absence of lesions outside of the thalami aid in narrowing the differential diagnosis,” and no systemic or extra-thalamic lesions were identified.
